etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English for, from Old English for (“for, because of”), from Proto-Germanic *furi (“for”), from Proto-Indo-European *preh₂-.

Cognate with West Frisian foar (“for”), Dutch voor (“for”), German für (“for”), Danish for (“for”), Swedish för (“for”), Norwegian for (“for”), Icelandic fyrir (“for”), Latin per (“by, through, for, by means of”) and Romance language successors (e.g. Spanish para (“for”)), Ancient Greek περί (perí, “for, about, toward”), Lithuanian per (“by, through, during”), Sanskrit परि (pári, “over, around”).

definitions.definition: (formal, literary) Because.

quote.citation: c. 1601, William Shakespeare, Twelfth Night‎[2], act 3, scene 4:
quote.text: […] Dismount thy tuck, be yare in thy preparation, for thy assailant is quick, skillful and deadly.

quote.citation: 1885, Richard Francis Burton, The Book of the Thousand Nights and a Night:
quote.text: […] nor is there found, in sea or on land, a sweeter or pleasanter of gifts than she; for she is prime in comeliness and seemlihead of face and symmetrical shape of perfect grace; her check is ruddy dight, her brow flower white, her teeth gem-bright, her eyes blackest black and whitest white, her hips of heavy weight, her waist slight and her favour exquisite.

quote.citation: 1900, L[yman] Frank Baum, chapter 23, in The Wonderful Wizard of Oz:
quote.text: "By means of the Golden Cap I shall command the Winged Monkeys to carry you to the gates of the Emerald City," said Glinda, "for it would be a shame to deprive the people of so wonderful a ruler."

definitions.definition: Towards; in the direction of.

quote.citation: 1627 (indicated as 1626), Francis [Bacon], “New Atlantis. A Worke Vnfinished.”, in Sylua Syluarum: Or A Naturall Historie. In Ten Centuries. […], London:  […]  William Rawley […]; [p]rinted by J[ohn] H[aviland] for William Lee […], →OCLC, page 1:
quote.text: Wee ſailed from Peru, (where wee had continued by the ſpace of one whole yeare,) for China and Iapan, by the South Sea; [...]

definitions.definition: Directed at; intended to belong to.
In order to help, benefit, gratify, honor etc. (someone or something).

quote.citation: 1976, Michael McDonald (lyrics and music), “Takin' It to the Streets”, performed by The Doobie Brothers:
quote.text: You, telling me the things you're gonna do for me.

definitions.definition: Befitting of someone’s beliefs, needs, wants, skills, or tastes; best suited to.
To be used or treated in a stated way, or with a stated purpose.
Supporting, in favour of.
Because of.

quote.citation: c. 1591–1592 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Third Part of Henry the Sixt, […]”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act II, scene v]:
quote.text: with fiery eyes sparkling for very wrath

quote.citation: 1867, Frederick Metcalfe, The Oxonian in Iceland, page 202:
quote.text: "A summerly day for you," said my host; "You ought to be here in winter. It is impossible then to get out of the doors for the snow and wind. Ugh! dreadful weather!"

quote.citation: 1864, George Etell Sargent, The Story of a City Arab, page 313:
quote.text: I could not see his hands, for the thick gloves he wore, and his face was partially concealed by a red woollen comforter; but his entire appearance and manners tallied with what I had seen of Yorkshire farmerhood.

definitions.definition: In order to cure, remove or counteract.
So as to allow (something or someone) to take position.
In anticipation of.
So as to identify or locate.
Over (a period of time).

quote.citation: 1717, Joseph Addison, Metamorphoses:
quote.text: To guide the sun's bright chariot for a day.

definitions.definition: Throughout or across (a distance in space).

quote.citation: c. 1603–1606, William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of King Lear”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act II, scene iv]:
quote.text: For many miles about / There's scarce a bush.

definitions.definition: Used to introduce a subject of a to-infinitive clause.
On behalf of.
In the role or capacity of; instead of; in place of.
In exchange for; in correspondence or equivalence with.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Exodus 21:23-24:
quote.text: And if any mischief follow, then thou shalt give life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot.

definitions.definition: In order to obtain or acquire.

quote.citation: 1641 (first performance), [John Denham], “The Prologue”, in The Sophy. […], 2nd edition, London:  […]  J[ohn] M[acock] for H[enry] Herringman, […], published 1667, →OCLC:
quote.text: For we would have you know it, / The loſs will fall on us, not on the Poet: / For he writes not for money, nor for praiſe, / Nor to be call'd a Wit, nor to wear Bayes:  […]

definitions.definition: By the standards of, usually with the implication that those standards are lower than one might otherwise expect; considering.
To be, or as being.

quote.citation: 17th century Abraham Cowley, Of Wit
quote.text: We take a falling meteor for a star.

quote.citation: a. 1705, John Locke, “Of the Conduct of the Understanding”, in Posthumous Works of Mr. John Locke: […], London:  […]  A[wnsham] and J[ohn] Churchill, […], published 1706, →OCLC:
quote.text: if a man can be persuaded and fully assured of anything for a truth without having examined, what is there that he may not embrace for truth ?

quote.citation: c. 1690, John Dryden, Translations (Preface)
quote.text: Most of our ingenious young men take up some cry'd-up English poet for their model.

quote.citation: 1712, Ambrose Philips, The Distrest Mother:
quote.text: But let her go for an ungrateful woman.

quote.citation: 1976, Louis L’Amour, chapter 2, in The Rider of Lost Creek, Bantam Dell, →ISBN:
quote.text: They knew him for a stranger.

definitions.definition: (usually in the phrase 'for all') Despite, in spite of.

quote.citation: 1898, H.G. Wells, The War of the Worlds, London: William Heinemann, page 113:
quote.text: "You must keep your head. There is still hope." "Hope!" "Yes; plentiful hope -- for all this destruction!"

quote.citation: 1892 August 6, "The Unbidden Guest", in Charles Dickens, Jr. (editor), All the Year Round,[3] page 133,
quote.text: Mr. Joseph Blenkinshaw was perhaps not worth quite so much as was reported; but for all that he was a very wealthy man  […]

quote.citation: 1968, J. J. Scarisbrick, Henry VIII, page 240:
quote.text: For all his faults, there had been something lofty and great about him - as a judge, as a patron of education, as a builder, as an international figure.

definitions.definition: Indicating something desired or anticipated.

quote.citation: 1599 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Life of Henry the Fift”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act PROLOGUE, (please specify the scene number in lowercase Roman numerals)]:
quote.text: O For a Muſe of Fire, that would aſcend / The brighteſt Heauen of Inuention :

quote.citation: 1858 March 27, “The Lay of the Brief”, in Punch, Or, The London Charivari, page 129:
quote.text: Oh! but to breathe the air / By their side under summer skies! To watch the blush on their cheeks, / The light in their liquid eyes. / Oh! but for one short hour, / To whisper a word of love;  […]

definitions.definition: (in expressions such as 'for a start') Introducing the first item(s) in a potential sequence .
(with names, chiefly US) In honor of; after.
(UK) Due for or facing (a certain outcome or fate).
(chiefly US) Out of; used to indicate a fraction, a ratio
(cricket) Used as part of a score to indicate the number of wickets that have fallen.
(obsolete) Indicating that in prevention of which, or through fear of which, anything is done.

quote.citation: 1609–1612, Francis Beaumont, John Fletcher, “The Captaine”, in Comedies and Tragedies […], London:  […]  Humphrey Robinson, […], and for Humphrey Moseley […], published 1647, →OCLC, Act III, scene v:
quote.text: We'll have a bib, for spoiling of thy doublet.

definitions.definition: (nonstandard) So (that), in order to

Used in various other more-or-less idiomatic ways to construe individual verbs, indicating various semantic relationships such as target, purpose, result, etc.; see also the entries for individual phrasal verbs, e.g. ask for, look for, stand for, etc.
